## 3.3 Next-token prediction and sampling

**Aim.** The reader understands that the model outputs a probability distribution over the next token, that text is generated by sampling one token at a time and feeding it back in, and what temperature and top-p sampling do.

**Text (draft).**

> At each position, the transformer's last layer produces a score, called a logit, for every token in the vocabulary. Softmax turns the scores into probabilities. During training this distribution is scored against the token that actually came next (Section 2.5).
>
> To generate text, the model computes the distribution for the next token, one token is sampled from it, the token is appended to the input, and the process repeats. Everything a chat model writes is produced this way, one token at a time.
>
> Two settings change the sampling. Temperature T divides the logits before softmax. T below 1 concentrates probability on the most likely tokens, and T above 1 spreads it out. Top-p sampling keeps only the most probable tokens whose probabilities add up to p, and samples among those.

**Formula.**

```latex
p_i = \frac{\exp(z_i / T)}{\sum_j \exp(z_j / T)}
```

**Image.** Bar charts of the ten most likely next tokens after "The capital of France is", at T = 0.5, 1, and 2.

**Interactive: "Sample the next token".**

- Display: a bar chart of the 20 most likely next tokens; the generated text so far, with each token's probability at the time it was chosen.
- Controls: prompt menu; temperature; top-p; Sample (one token); Greedy (take the most likely); Reset.
- Try: (1) Generate at T = 0 several times and compare. (2) Generate at T = 1.5 and watch the text drift. (3) Find a prompt where the model is nearly certain and one where it is unsure.
- What to notice: any one answer from a model is a single draw from a distribution.
- Build: live with a small model run in the browser (distilgpt2 through transformers.js), with a precomputed fallback; medium.

**Check.** At a temperature near 0, what does sampling become? Answer: always choosing the most likely token (greedy decoding).

**Links.** Back to 2.5; forward to 4.3 (changing the distribution with a reward). References: Holtzman et al. (2020), on top-p sampling.
